rag_semantic_descriptions: An automated tool is rapidly and repeatedly attempting to log in to the SSH service on port 22 by systematically guessing passwords from a dictionary or credential list.
The traffic shows thousands of short-lived TCP connections to port 22, each following the same pattern: cryptographic handshake, authentication attempt, server rejection, immediate disconnect.
Despite the encrypted SSH payload making content inspection impossible, the attack is identifiable by the rapid-fire connection establishment and teardown pattern targeting port 22.
Each individual network flow has an extremely short duration because the SSH server drops the connection the moment authentication fails, and the automated tool instantly starts a new attempt.
The packet size sequencing is highly uniform across thousands of flows — each follows the same predictable structure of key exchange, authentication guess, rejection response, and teardown.
The inter-arrival time between connection attempts is minimal, reflecting machine-speed automated scripting rather than a human administrator typing passwords manually.
The forward packet rate is very high as the tool aggressively initiates new SSH connections, while the server responses are relatively low-volume since they only send rejection messages.
Advanced attackers may distribute the brute force across multiple source IPs or introduce deliberate timing delays to evade threshold-based protections like fail2ban.
This could be confused with legitimate automation like Ansible, Puppet, or backup scripts using expired SSH keys, which also generate bursts of failed login attempts.
The attack targets the most common remote administration protocol and relies on weak or default passwords, making it one of the most frequently observed credential attacks on the internet.
